title: Privacy law can shut newsrooms: media body; SC notice to Centre
syllabus: GS2 › Fundamental rights (Art 19, Art 21); Judiciary · GS3 › Data protection; Challenges to internal security through communication networks · GS4 › Right to information, privacy and media ethics
summary: The Supreme Court issued notice to the Centre on a news publishers' petition that the DPDP Act, 2023 and Rules, 2025 give no exemption for journalism; hearing on 17 November.
evolution: K S Puttaswamy: a nine-judge bench holds privacy a fundamental right.
Earlier drafts of the data protection law excluded journalism, the petitioners say.
Digital Personal Data Protection Act passed, with no journalism exemption.
SC issues notice on the Digital News Publishers Association's plea; also on a stay application.
ideas: Two fundamental rights collide: privacy (Art 21, Puttaswamy) and press freedom (Art 19(1)(a)); the law must balance, not choose.
The DPDP challenge pits privacy under Article 21 against press freedom under Article 19(1)(a); the Constitution demands balance, not hierarchy.
A consent-based regime clashes with news: needing a subject's prior consent amounts to pre-censorship; the press answers for errors after publication.
Requiring a subject's consent before reporting is prior restraint; press accountability should come after publication, as in defamation law.
The chilling effect reaches beyond newsrooms, to citizen journalists, whistleblowers and RTI activists.
Without a journalistic exemption, the DPDP Act could chill not just newsrooms but whistleblowers and RTI activists, the watchdogs of democracy.
keywords: Proportionality test
Puttaswamy's test: legality, legitimate aim, proportionality
Any rights-restriction answer
Any restriction on press freedom must pass Puttaswamy's proportionality test: legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.
Chilling effect
Fear of legal action that deters lawful speech
Free speech answers
Vague, consent-based obligations create a chilling effect on investigative journalism.
Prior restraint / pre-censorship
Stopping speech before it is published
Press freedom answers
Courts have long treated prior restraint as the gravest restriction on free speech.
Journalistic exemption
Carve-out allowing news processing of personal data
Data protection answers
A narrowly drawn journalistic exemption, as in the EU's GDPR, would reconcile privacy with press freedom.
Data principal / data fiduciary
The person whose data it is / the entity processing it
DPDP Act answers
The DPDP Act treats a newspaper reporting on a person as a data fiduciary needing the data principal's consent.
Fourth estate
The press as democracy's watchdog
Conclusion
A free press, the fourth estate, needs room to report without the subject's permission.
examples: K S Puttaswamy v Union of India (2017)
Privacy declared a fundamental right; proportionality test laid down
Privacy and its limits
Puttaswamy (2017) made privacy a fundamental right but also allowed proportionate restrictions.
Shreya Singhal v Union of India (2015)
SC struck down Section 66A of the IT Act for vagueness and chilling effect
Free speech
As in Shreya Singhal (2015), vague curbs that chill speech fail Article 19.
EU GDPR, Article 85
Requires member states to reconcile data protection with journalism
Global best practice
The EU's GDPR (Art 85) obliges states to reconcile data protection with freedom of expression and journalism.
pyqs: Directly on the DPDP Act: add the missing journalistic exemption and today's challenge as a criticism.
Puttaswamy's privacy right now meets Article 19(1)(a): the DPDP petition is a live test of its scope.
Privacy under Article 21 is not absolute; it must be balanced against press freedom.
Privacy as self-identity under Article 21; the DPDP case shows the other side, privacy versus the public's right to know.
Shreya Singhal and Section 66A: vague restrictions with a chilling effect, the same argument the publishers now make.
Limits of free speech: the same Article 19 now invoked by the press against a privacy law.
The Srikrishna-era draft excluded journalism, the petitioners say; the final Act did not.
Transparency institutions under pressure: RTI activists are among those the petition says the Act will affect.

trend.t: Rights questions follow one pattern: a right is stated, then tested against a specific law or competing claim. Free speech was tested against Section 66A (2013) and hate speech (2014); Article 21 against bursting crackers (2015). After Puttaswamy, privacy took centre stage: its scope (2017), then privacy against a paternity DNA test (2024) and self-identity under the 2026 amendment to the Transgender Persons Act (2026). GS III asks the same right as data law: Srikrishna Committee (2018), DPDP Act (2024).
trend.watch: Privacy under Article 21 has come three times in GS II (2017, 2024, 2026) and twice as data protection in GS III (2018, 2024). The favourite format is a right in conflict with another right or interest, so privacy versus other fundamental rights is a must-study area.

answer.t: On 27 October 2026 the Supreme Court sought the Centre's response to a plea that the DPDP Act, 2023 and Rules, 2025 offer no exemption for journalism, pitting Article 21 privacy against Article 19(1)(a).

answer.h: The tension: how a data protection law can curb the press

pts.t: Processing personal data needs the person's consent, so a story on a public figure could need his permission.
pts.ex: Counsel told the SC this would 'shut down the newsroom'.

pts.t: Obligations before publication act as pre-censorship, the gravest curb on speech.
Subjects could demand deletion of inconvenient but true reports, eroding the public record.
Citizen journalists, whistleblowers and RTI activists face the same duties as corporations.
Treating journalism like commercial data processing ignores its distinct constitutional role.
The Act lets the Centre exempt its own agencies, but not the press.
Privacy and speech are both subject to reasonable restrictions.
Any restriction needs legality, a legitimate aim and the least restrictive means.
Reporting on public conduct deserves protection; purely private life deserves privacy.
pts.ex: R Rajagopal v State of TN (1994).

pts.t: Remedies for false or harmful reporting should follow publication, not block it.
Vague duties that chill speech fail Article 19.
Data laws carve out journalism with safeguards.
A broad exemption may shield fake news outlets or data brokers posing as media.
Paparazzi intrusion and media trials can violate privacy and fair trial.
Online reports stay searchable forever, raising 'right to be forgotten' claims.
Press Council has limited powers and none over digital media.
The Data Protection Board is appointed by the Centre, raising fears of selective action.
Pending challenges leave newsrooms in legal uncertainty.
Exempt processing for journalism in the public interest, with safeguards.
Codify when privacy yields to the public's right to know.
Keep data security duties for media, drop consent and erasure for news.
A statutory media council covering print and digital, with an ethics code.
Insulate appointments and tenure from executive control.
SC guidelines on the balance, as in Puttaswamy, until Parliament amends.

answer.t: A narrowly drawn journalistic exemption, tested by proportionality and public interest, can protect both the individual's privacy and the citizen's right to know.

title: When courts are too slow, police replace judges
syllabus: GS2 › Structure, organisation and functioning of the judiciary; Police reforms · GS4 › Probity in governance
context: Abhinav Chandrachud argues that years-long civil suits push well-connected litigants to the police, who turn debt and contract disputes into criminal cases of 'cheating' or 'breach of trust'. This creates a parallel, coercive civil-justice system.
ideas: Delay breeds a 'parallel justice' system: police summons and threats of arrest replace a court's verdict.
Judicial delay has bred 'parallel justice', with police summons and arrest threats replacing a court's verdict in civil disputes.
The root is too few judges: about 15 per million people in Maharashtra against about 157 in New York state.
Maharashtra has about 15 judges per million people against about 157 in New York state; vacancies feed delay.
Using criminal law to settle a civil debt is abuse of process; the Supreme Court has discouraged it, but practice lags the law.
GS2 rule of law · GS4 probity
Turning a civil debt into a criminal case is abuse of process, discouraged by the Supreme Court but common in practice.
keywords: Criminalisation of civil disputes
Turning debt or contract quarrels into 'cheating' cases
Police reforms
The criminalisation of civil disputes shows police discretion being misused for private ends.
Abuse of process
Using legal procedure for an improper aim
Misuse of criminal law
Using criminal law to recover a debt is a textbook abuse of process.
Justice delayed is justice denied
Delay itself defeats the purpose of justice
Pendency introduction
A Bombay HC suit filed in 1947 settled only in 2026: justice delayed is justice denied.
Law in the books vs law in action
The gap between what the law says and how it works
Conclusion
Reform must close the gap between law in the books and law in action.
data: Judges per million people: Maharashtra vs New York state
With about 15 judges per million in Maharashtra against about 157 in New York state, India's courts are short-staffed.

The officer who refuses an influential complainant

GS4 · Integrity

pyqs: Free legal aid is not enough if justice takes decades: cite the 79-year Bombay HC suit and ~15 judges per million in Maharashtra against ~157 in New York state.
Argue for Lok Adalats and ADR: when civil suits take 20+ years, settlements move to police stations instead.
Rule of law: 'law on the books' versus 'law in action' when police turn debt disputes into criminal cases.
The police-as-debt-collector trend shows why probity matters for governance and public trust.
summary: Slow civil courts are pushing creditors to the police, who turn money disputes into criminal cases to force a settlement (Abhinav Chandrachud).
evolution: The Privy Council observed that a litigant's troubles in India begin when he has obtained a decree.
A Bombay High Court suit took 79 years before it was settled out of court.
